stories.headline: China Postpones Chang'e-7 Moon Mission, Potentially Leveling Space Race
stories.summary:
China has postponed the launch of its Chang'e-7 lunar mission, which had been expected to lift off as early as Sunday, according to the China Manned Space Engineering Office. State media announced the delay citing that the probe does not meet launch conditions, following an assessment guided by the principle of 'prudence, reliability and absolute mission success.' The precise technical reason was not disclosed.

Chang'e-7 was designed to hunt for water ice at the moon's south pole — a resource both Beijing and Washington consider critical for future deep-space exploration, potential lunar settlements, and even rocket fuel production. No mission has yet directly analyzed lunar water on the surface; China's probe would have been the first to attempt it.

The delay could offer the United States a window to close the gap in this chapter of the space race. Pittsburgh-based Astrobotic Technologies is targeting a late 2026 south pole landing with its Griffin lander, and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin plans to send robotic landers — potentially including NASA's VIPER water-hunting rover — to the same region as early as next year.

Lunar scientists say the question of whether south pole water ice exists in quantities useful for a permanent base remains open. Brown University professor James Head, a NASA Apollo program veteran, said Chang'e-7 could have made 'important progress on this question'; the delay now shifts that opportunity back toward American and commercial missions.

stories.headline: Sean Grayson, Ex-Deputy Convicted of Killing Sonya Massey, Dies in Prison at 32
stories.summary:
Sean Grayson, the former Sangamon County, Illinois sheriff's deputy sentenced to 20 years for the second-degree murder of Sonya Massey, died early Sunday in prison at age 32, his defense attorney Daniel Fultz confirmed. Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer prior to the 2024 shooting and the disease had advanced to his liver and lungs by January 2026. An Illinois Prisoner Review Board voted unanimously in July to deny his application for early medical release.

Grayson shot Massey, a 36-year-old Black single mother, in the face on July 6, 2024, after she called 911 about a possible prowler. Body camera footage showed Grayson yelling at Massey as she moved a pot of hot water from the stove; she said 'I'm sorry' and ducked before he fired three times. Grayson argued he feared she would scald him. He was convicted in October 2024 and received the maximum sentence in January 2026.

The shooting drew nationwide protests over systemic racism and prompted a U.S. Department of Justice review. Grayson's death means he served approximately six months of his sentence. It is not yet confirmed whether his death was directly cancer-related.

Attorneys Ben Crump and Antonio Romanucci, representing Massey's family, issued a statement Sunday extending prayers to Grayson's family while stressing that 'Sonya Massey's death was unjustifiable, and she should be alive today. Sean Grayson's death in custody from cancer does not bring Sonya back.'

stories.headline: Trump Reconciles Publicly with Michael Cohen in Wide-Ranging Radio Interview
stories.summary:
President Trump and former personal attorney Michael Cohen have publicly reconciled, conducting a friendly interview that aired in full on Sunday — the first time the two have spoken publicly since Cohen became a key prosecution witness against Trump in his New York criminal hush-money trial. The interview covered topics including Trump's economic record, a proposed White House ballroom project, and what Trump called the 'weaponization' of government against political opponents.

Cohen pleaded guilty in 2018 to federal crimes including campaign finance violations and served prison time. He subsequently became one of Trump's most prominent and vocal critics, testifying in multiple proceedings against his former boss. Their public rapprochement is a notable political reversal given the bitterness of their falling-out and Cohen's central role in legal cases that dogged Trump's return to power.

Supporters of Trump are likely to view the reconciliation as a demonstration of Trump's dominance over adversaries and vindication of his claims that prosecutions were politically motivated. Critics may question Cohen's motivations, given his history of shifting loyalties, and some legal analysts have noted that the interview could have implications for any ongoing proceedings in which Cohen's credibility as a witness remains relevant.

The interview also touched on Trump's defense of AI data centers, with the president telling Cohen the U.S. is leading China in artificial intelligence 'by a lot' and that data centers were building their own power rather than drawing from the grid — remarks that diverge from criticism by Republican governors including Texas's Greg Abbott.

stories.headline: Jared Kushner Met Privately with House Democratic Leader Jeffries, Speaker Johnson Downplays Significance
stories.summary:
Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, held a private meeting with House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), The New York Times first reported Sunday. The conversation spanned issues including housing, immigration, and the cost of living. The meeting is notable given Jeffries is widely expected to become House Speaker if Democrats reclaim the majority in November's midterm elections.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the meeting in a Fox News appearance Sunday, saying he did not know its purpose and that Kushner is 'not really directly involved' in the Trump administration. Kushner has maintained a lower public profile during Trump's second term compared to the first, though he retains close family ties to the president.

The meeting has drawn attention because it suggests Kushner may be positioning himself as an informal back-channel between the White House and a potential future Democratic House leadership. Democrats are favored to retake the House in November, which would hand Jeffries the speakership and create divided government for the final two years of Trump's term.

Neither Kushner's office nor Jeffries' office immediately provided detailed comment on the substance or purpose of the discussions. The nature of any potential policy collaboration between Kushner and Democratic leadership remains unclear.

stories.headline: Border Patrol Arrests Father of Active-Duty Navy Sailor Awaiting Son's Return from Record Deployment
stories.summary:
Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, a Nicaraguan-born handyman who has lived in the United States for 19 years, was arrested by Border Patrol in Key West, Florida, on Saturday while his son was serving aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln — a vessel that set a U.S. military record for uninterrupted time at sea, surpassing nine months of deployment. Aviles' wife says her husband holds a work permit and was simply taking his car to a mechanic when agents detained him. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed the arrest and said Aviles will remain in ICE custody pending deportation proceedings.

The arrest is part of a broader pattern documented by the Associated Press, which found that the Trump administration has detained at least dozens of parents and spouses of active-duty service members as part of its mass deportation agenda. At least six such family members have been deported, one self-deported, and one spouse was pulled off a deportation flight to Brazil after AP reporting drew public attention. The administration has rolled back "military parole-in-place" protections, a longstanding immigration benefit allowing relatives of service members to pursue legal status from within the country.

The Trump administration defended the arrests, with the Department of Homeland Security stating: "Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation's laws." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had previously dismissed concerns about conditions aboard the Lincoln as "completely misrepresented," even as reports surfaced of food shortages, equipment strain, and deteriorating mental health among sailors on the extended deployment.

Critics argue the detentions undermine military morale and retention at a time when the armed forces are already stretched. The case raises broader questions about the scope of deportation enforcement and its intersection with military families, a constituency that has historically enjoyed bipartisan protection from immigration hardship.

stories.headline: CMS Chief Oz Contradicts Trump, Says MMR Vaccine 'Is Not a Lethal Vaccine'
stories.summary:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, publicly broke with President Trump on Sunday, stating flatly that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is "not a lethal vaccine" and that it is offered in countries around the world. Oz was pressed three times on CBS News's "Face the Nation" to address claims Trump made earlier this month suggesting the MMR vaccine posed lethal risks — remarks that drew widespread alarm from public health officials and pediatricians.

Trump's comments on MMR had already stoked concern among medical groups who warned that presidential statements casting doubt on widely administered childhood vaccines could depress vaccination rates and fuel outbreaks. The U.S. has already seen measles cases rise in recent years, and health officials have urged federal leaders to send unambiguous messages in support of established vaccine safety records.

Oz's public rebuttal is notable given his role overseeing Medicare and Medicaid and his position within a administration that has shown skepticism toward vaccine mandates and certain public health institutions. His willingness to contradict the president on a nationally televised Sunday program signals tension within the administration over health messaging, particularly as the country approaches flu and respiratory virus season.

The episode underscores a recurring friction in the Trump administration between political figures who have questioned mainstream vaccine guidance and career or appointed health officials who continue to align with scientific consensus. No response from the White House was immediately available.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Details Rift with Dismissed Defense Minister, Discloses Patriot Missile Shortage
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly detailed for the first time his dispute with dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov during a two-hour off-the-record briefing with reporters on Saturday, the transcript of which was released Sunday. Zelensky said he had offered Fedorov four separate positions within the government after removing him, all of which Fedorov rejected, and characterized Fedorov's subsequent involvement in mass protests and calls for wartime elections as misguided. He also alleged that inaccurate information from the Defense Ministry contributed to an embarrassing diplomatic episode involving Starlink use in Russia.

A significant new disclosure from Zelensky concerns Ukraine's dwindling stock of Patriot air-defense missiles. The president revealed data showing that deliveries from Western allies have declined over the past three years even as Russian ballistic missile strikes have intensified, leaving Ukraine increasingly exposed. He also said Ukrainian forces have nearly fully recaptured the Dnipropetrovsk region, with only about 10 square kilometers still under Russian control — a rare battlefield gain he described as meaningful.

Fedorov, credited with modernizing Ukraine's military and accelerating its drone warfare capabilities, was dismissed last month after reportedly falling out with the country's top military commander. His removal triggered weeks of mass protests that failed to reverse the decision. He has since called publicly for elections, a position Zelensky reiterated he strongly opposes, describing wartime elections as a potential "tsunami" that could split the country apart.

The remarks represent the most detailed account yet from Zelensky on both the political crisis surrounding Fedorov's ouster and the state of Ukraine's air defenses — a topic with direct implications for ongoing Western military aid negotiations.

stories.headline: Trump Waves Green Flag at First-Ever IndyCar Race Through Washington Streets, Closing Out U.S. 250th Birthday Events
stories.summary:
President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump completed a ceremonial lap of a 1.7-mile street circuit in Washington, D.C., on Sunday before waving the green flag to start the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the first professional road race ever held in the nation's capital. Trump's new Air Force One performed a flyover as the lap concluded. American driver Kyle Kirkwood won the 250-mile race, earning his seventh career IndyCar victory, as drivers reached speeds of up to 190 mph past the Washington Monument and the U.S. Capitol.

The event drew an estimated 140,000 spectators, many of whom received free general admission tickets through a public lottery, though premium packages were priced at $5,000 per pair. The race required extensive city preparation, including manholes being bolted shut, road resurfacing, and a three-hour airspace closure over Reagan National Airport to accommodate the military flyover. The National Gallery of Art conducted vibration tests to protect its collection from engine noise.

The Grand Prix served as the capstone of a summer-long series of events organized around the United States' 250th anniversary. Earlier celebrations included a UFC event on the White House lawn and a July Fourth fireworks display. The administration framed the events as a celebration of American achievement and patriotism.

For the city of Washington and for the IndyCar series, the race represented an unusual convergence of motorsport and national symbolism. American driver Josef Newgarden called racing through the capital "very surreal" and said the moment "might never happen again."

stories.headline: Landfill Collapse in Guinea's Capital Kills at Least 30
stories.summary:
A massive mound of rubbish collapsed onto homes in the Dar-es-Salam neighborhood of Conakry, Guinea, killing at least 30 people and injuring 22 others, including six critically. The collapse occurred around 2:00 a.m. local time following heavy overnight rain, catching residents asleep in their homes. One woman told local media that all five of her children perished in the disaster, and officials fear the death toll will rise as search efforts continue.

Guinea's government deployed significant resources to the scene, including military personnel and excavators to comb through the debris. Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah visited the site to oversee the rescue operation. A neighborhood leader said 18 bodies had already been retrieved and transported to the morgue by Sunday morning.

The incident highlights chronic waste management failures in rapidly urbanizing African capitals, where informal settlements frequently develop near large landfill sites. A previous landslide at the same Conakry waste site killed 10 people in 2017, raising questions about why residential construction was permitted to continue in proximity to the hazard.

stories.headline: Texas Gov. Abbott Says AI Data Center Companies 'Dug Their Own Grave' as Backlash Grows
stories.summary:
Texas Governor Greg Abbott issued one of the sharpest rebukes yet from a Republican executive toward the artificial intelligence industry, telling ABC News that data center companies 'dug their own grave' by failing to build community support for their projects. Abbott earlier this month imposed a moratorium on new data center development in Texas pending a state regulatory audit of proposed sites seeking grid connections. The reversal is striking given Abbott's prior enthusiastic courting of the industry as a driver of economic growth.

Abbott joins a bipartisan wave of governors pulling back from the data center boom, including Democratic Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, as local opposition has transformed into a potent electoral issue ahead of the November midterms. Candidates in both parties are campaigning against data centers, citing concerns over energy demand, water usage, noise, and land use. Separately, AI-powered license plate reader cameras, known as Flock cameras, have emerged as a parallel flashpoint, with grassroots anger over surveillance technology also influencing races across the country.

The backlash represents a significant political realignment. The AI buildout was until recently treated as an unambiguous economic boon by officials in both parties eager to attract investment and jobs. Critics of the industry argue data centers strain power grids and local infrastructure while delivering relatively few permanent jobs; supporters counter that the facilities are essential to U.S. technological competitiveness and national security. The midterm environment has accelerated the shift in political calculus for incumbents in affected communities.

stories.headline: Update: Stars and Stripes Editor Speaks Out on Censorship Fears After Pentagon Firing
stories.summary:
Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief Erik Slavin has spoken publicly for the first time since being dismissed by the Department of Defense for 'insubordination,' telling the BBC he fears a chilling effect on coverage of the U.S. military. Slavin said he believes his firing stemmed from a CBS interview in which he stated that censorship would be a 'red line' in a hypothetical scenario. The paper's publisher Max Lederer and Middle East reporter Lara Korte were also dismissed; Korte said on X that the firings were 'a shame for the institution and service members, who swore to defend the Constitution.'

Slavin said he was not given an official explanation for his dismissal and has no right of appeal. He noted the firing occurred in a climate where the Pentagon has held no press conference since May and has repeatedly sought to influence editorial decisions. He said he did not know definitively whether the terminations were linked to Stars and Stripes reporting on conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, a carrier deployed in the Gulf for a record-breaking 240-plus days with reported sailor mental health crises.

The Pentagon declined to comment to the BBC. The National Press Club president called the firing 'another brazen attempt by the Pentagon to dictate coverage of the military.' Stars and Stripes, which reaches an average of 1.4 million readers daily, holds a congressional mandate for editorial independence even as it receives partial Pentagon funding — a tension that now appears to be at the center of a broader dispute over press freedom within the armed forces.

stories.headline: Indiana Utility Faces Class-Action Lawsuit as Nearly 30,000 Remain Without Power 12 Days After Storms
stories.summary:
Nearly 30,000 customers in northern Indiana remained without electricity as of Sunday, twelve days after severe storms packing wind gusts of up to 99 mph struck the region on August 11, killing seven people. The utility Northern Indiana Public Service Company (Nipsco) has restored power to more than 345,000 customers since the storm, but restoration efforts have been slow in the hardest-hit areas, including the city of Gary, where a third of the roughly 70,000 residents live in poverty. Residents have reported being unable to refrigerate medication, a wheelchair user navigating darkened stairwells, and streets 'pitch black' at night without functioning streetlights.

Frustration with Nipsco's response has escalated to legal action, with local residents launching a class-action lawsuit accusing the company of failing to adequately manage its infrastructure. The global food charity World Central Kitchen deployed to the area after petrol stations, supermarkets, and pharmacies lost power in the immediate aftermath, leaving many without access to food. Elderly and disabled residents have been among the most vulnerable, with some reporting they have been relying on neighbors and family for basic necessities.

The prolonged outage has renewed scrutiny of utility grid resilience in aging Midwestern industrial communities. Gary was once home to the world's largest steel mill and remains one of the most economically distressed cities in the region, a combination that has amplified the human cost of an infrastructure failure that, while precipitated by an unusual storm, has exposed longstanding vulnerabilities in the local power network.

stories.headline: DR Congo and M23 Rebels Agree Roadmap for Peace Talks After Five Days of Swiss Negotiations
stories.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed Sunday to a formal roadmap for peace negotiations following five days of talks in Switzerland. In a joint statement, both parties pledged to pursue comprehensive peace and conflict resolution under a US-brokered framework first signed in 2025, and established a mechanism to monitor the existing ceasefire.

The agreement sets out sequenced timelines for negotiations but leaves significant disagreements unresolved, including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees, and the timing of political reforms. A ceasefire monitoring secretariat has been established, with the first verification mission scheduled for Monday in Minembwe, an area of South Kivu where fighting has continued despite prior commitments.

The conflict, which intensified in January 2025 when M23 seized parts of eastern DRC including the city of Goma, has killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians. Rwanda denies backing M23 with troops and weapons, calling its regional military presence defensive, while DRC accuses Kigali of direct involvement. Eastern DRC's vast reserves of coltan and other minerals critical to global electronics supply chains give the conflict broad international economic significance.

stories.headline: DOJ Maneuver on Unconfirmed U.S. Attorneys Inches Closer to Supreme Court
stories.summary:
A Justice Department practice of installing acting U.S. attorneys without Senate confirmation is moving toward a potential Supreme Court showdown after two federal appeals court panels ruled last week that the DOJ cannot circumvent the confirmation process by changing an official's title or reassigning the duties of the top prosecutor.

The rulings constrain the administration's use of the Federal Vacancies Reform Act to place loyalists in key prosecutorial roles without going through Congress. Critics, including Democratic lawmakers and legal scholars, argue the maneuver undermines the Senate's constitutional advice-and-consent role and allows the executive branch to concentrate prosecutorial power without accountability. Administration supporters contend the president has broad authority to staff the executive branch and that the FVRA provides lawful flexibility during vacancies.

With two circuit courts now ruling against the DOJ's approach, the stage is set for the Supreme Court to weigh in on the scope of executive appointment power — a question with significant implications for how future administrations staff federal law enforcement positions across the country.

stories.headline: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, First Woman Elected to Senate in Her Own Right, Dies at 94
stories.summary:
Former Republican Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker of Kansas, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without having previously been preceded by a husband who held the seat, died Friday of natural causes at age 94. Her son Bill Kassebaum confirmed the death to the Associated Press, describing her as 'an independent-minded Republican who was willing to stand up for what she thought was right, even if that meant going against the party.'

Kassebaum Baker won her Senate seat in 1978 and served three terms through 1997, the daughter of former Kansas Gov. Alf Landon, the Republican Party's 1936 presidential nominee. She chaired the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and was known for bipartisan work, most notably the landmark 1996 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, known as the Kennedy-Kassebaum bill, co-authored with Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy of Massachusetts.

Over her career she supported an assault weapons ban and later endorsed Democratic candidates in Kansas races, reflecting a moderate Republicanism increasingly at odds with the party's direction. She remained broadly popular in Kansas, winning re-election with 76% of the vote in 1984 and 74% in 1990. In 1996 she married former Republican Sen. Howard Baker of Tennessee, marking the first marriage between two individuals who had each served in the Senate.

stories.headline: Zelensky Denies Ukraine's Role in Nord Stream Sabotage Following Second Suspect Arrest in Croatia
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that Ukraine played no role in the 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, following Croatia's arrest of a second Ukrainian suspect sought by German authorities investigating the attack. The denial came as German prosecutors continue to build a case linking Ukrainian nationals to the underwater explosions that ruptured the pipelines linking Russia to Western Europe.

Germany has been pursuing multiple suspects in the investigation and the arrest in Croatia marks a significant development in an inquiry that has drawn in intelligence services from several countries. Russia has long alleged Western or Ukrainian involvement, while earlier reporting pointed to a private Ukrainian-linked operation. Ukraine has consistently denied any state involvement.

The Nord Stream sabotage has remained one of the most consequential and contested acts of infrastructure destruction in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine, with the pipelines' destruction eliminating a major energy route at a time of acute European energy insecurity. The question of accountability carries significant geopolitical weight for NATO unity, German-Ukrainian relations, and the broader prosecution of the war.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Rejects Wartime Elections, Calls Them a 'Tsunami' That Would Split Ukraine
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly rejected calls for wartime elections on Sunday, saying they would pose a "huge risk" and act as a "tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine." His remarks came four days after sacked Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov posted a video demanding that Ukraine be given a mechanism to hold democratic elections even amid the ongoing war with Russia.

Fedorov, who was fired in mid-July amid a reported feud with top general Oleksandr Syrskyi, told the BBC on Sunday that Zelensky had "questions to answer" about alleged corruption in his government, referencing a money laundering investigation announced last week. Fedorov said Ukrainians should not fear discussing elections, arguing that democracy "cannot be held hostage by Russia." Zelensky imposed martial law when Russia invaded in February 2022, legally prohibiting elections from being held.

The standoff marks the most significant public challenge to Zelensky's authority since the war began. Fedorov, widely credited with dramatically expanding Ukraine's long-range drone strike capabilities and deepening Russia's domestic vulnerabilities, commanded broad public respect, and his July dismissal triggered weeks of street protests across Ukraine.

The dispute highlights growing internal tensions in Kyiv over governance and accountability even as the war continues. Supporters of Zelensky argue elections during active conflict would be exploited by Russia and could destabilize the front lines; critics, including Fedorov, contend that postponing democratic accountability indefinitely undermines the very values Ukraine claims to be defending.

stories.headline: Hawk Fire Near Reno Forces Nearly 14,000 Homes to Evacuate as Blaze Reaches 0% Containment
stories.summary:
A fast-moving wildfire erupted near Reno, Nevada on Saturday and rapidly spread toward the city's core, forcing evacuation orders for nearly 14,000 homes by Sunday morning. The Hawk Fire grew to more than 10,500 acres and was zero percent contained as of Sunday, with "GO NOW" evacuation zones reaching the edge of the University of Nevada campus. Strong gusty winds, low humidity, and dry vegetation drove the blaze's rapid spread.

Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the Nevada National Guard, deploying two helicopter crews and 60 troops to support aerial firefighting and neighborhood security. Nearly 10,000 homes and businesses lost power in the county, and portions of U.S. Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed. Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve urged residents under evacuation orders not to delay, noting that structures had already burned.

The fire marks the second significant wildfire emergency near Reno this month. Earlier in August, three separate wildfires north of the city forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes. The repeated events underscore worsening fire conditions across the drought-stressed Great Basin region.

Evacuees were directed to the Reno-Sparks Convention Center, with separate facilities designated for pets and large animals. Officials described the situation as "very dynamic" and warned conditions remained dangerous as firefighters worked to prevent the fire from advancing further into residential neighborhoods.

stories.headline: Update: Iran's New Security Chief Threatens Gulf States, Vows to 'Neutralize' U.S. Economic War
stories.summary:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei issued a stark warning to neighboring Gulf states on Sunday, threatening to "target their interests" if any of them cooperate with the United States' escalating economic pressure campaign. Rezaei also vowed to halt oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz should neighboring countries join the U.S. economic crackdown, a threat that would affect a substantial share of global crude oil shipments. The U.S. is expected to detail new expanded sanctions against Tehran on Monday.

Rezaei also declared that the U.S. campaign of "maximum economic pressure" would fail, while Iran's president acknowledged the country's significant economic difficulties stemming from the ongoing conflict and sanctions regime. The Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since succeeding his father earlier this year, was the subject of newly released footage by an Iranian news site, though the clips appeared to be undated archive material, sustaining questions about his health and condition.

Separately, British energy companies were placed on alert after hackers believed to be affiliated with the Iranian government temporarily shut down a small-scale UK energy generator last month, according to reporting by The Sunday Telegraph. The plant was closed for four days due to the intrusion. Britain's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero wrote to energy companies with security guidance, though a government spokesperson said the attack posed no threat to the broader energy system.

The escalating rhetoric and cyber activity illustrate how the U.S.-Iran conflict is extending beyond direct military confrontation to economic warfare and infrastructure targeting. The Hormuz threat in particular draws attention given prior coverage indicating that oil markets have grown somewhat skeptical of such warnings, though energy companies are taking the cyber dimension increasingly seriously.

stories.headline: Tropical Storm Moke Advances Toward Hawaii, Threatening Islands Already Battered by Hurricane Lala
stories.summary:
Tropical Storm Moke was advancing toward Hawaii on Saturday, threatening to deliver additional heavy rainfall and damaging winds to the Big Island just days after Hurricane Lala left widespread destruction in its wake. As of Saturday morning, Moke was located approximately 470 miles southeast of Hilo, moving west-northwest at 12 mph with maximum sustained winds of around 50 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center.

The Big Island is expected to bear the brunt of the storm, with forecasts calling for 5 to 10 inches of rain on the southeast and windward sides and up to 15 inches in isolated areas. Forecasters warned of the potential for dangerous rip currents, life-threatening flooding, and mudslides, particularly in steep terrain where the ground remains saturated from Lala. Roughly 9,000 customers on the island remained without power from the previous storm as Moke approached.

Hurricane Lala, which struck earlier in the week, downed trees, swept buildings off their foundations, damaged roads and bridges, and deposited mud and rocks across roadways. The northeast coast of the Big Island recorded a staggering 43.54 inches of total rainfall from Lala. One storm-related death was reported. Communities are still in active cleanup and recovery mode.

Hawaii Governor Josh Green held a news conference urging residents to restock food, medicine, and other essentials before Moke's arrival. Meteorologists said the new storm's impacts would likely be somewhat more limited than Lala's but warned that the already-saturated ground and damaged infrastructure significantly increase the risk of serious secondary effects from even moderate additional rainfall.

stories.headline: USPS Issues Rule Tightening Mail-In Ballot Requirements Ahead of Midterms Despite Court Injunction
stories.summary:
The United States Postal Service on Friday announced new eligibility guidelines for mail-in ballots, moving to comply with President Trump's March executive order restricting the practice even though a federal court has struck down that order. The USPS's 95-page unpublished rule, set for official release August 26, details how the agency would distribute mail-in ballots for November's midterm elections and requires states to share voter lists.

The rule is already facing legal challenge: a federal injunction on Trump's underlying executive order remains in effect, putting the two directives in direct conflict. The collision between the administrative rule and the court order sets up a significant legal dispute over voting procedures with midterm elections approaching.

Supporters of the restrictions argue they are necessary to ensure ballot integrity and reduce fraud risks in mail-in voting. Critics and voting-rights advocates contend the rule is an effort to suppress participation, particularly among groups that rely heavily on mail-in ballots, and that the USPS is acting in defiance of a valid court order. The dispute is expected to escalate in federal courts in the coming days before the rule's scheduled publication.

stories.headline: More Than 50 Coordinated Arson Attacks Strike Southern Thailand Amid Long-Running Insurgency
stories.summary:
Thai military authorities reported that more than 50 coordinated arson and incendiary attacks struck Thailand's insurgency-affected southern border provinces late Saturday, with incidents concentrated in Narathiwat, Yala, and Pattani. Targets included a local government office building, telecommunication towers, a convenience store, and stolen vehicles. At least two women were injured when a bomb exploded in Narathiwat's Muang district.

Authorities imposed an overnight curfew in Narathiwat province, which was lifted Sunday morning after no further attacks were reported. Security officials warned residents not to touch suspicious objects as investigators assessed the scope of the coordinated campaign. No group has claimed responsibility.

The attacks are the latest episode in a low-level separatist conflict that has simmered in Thailand's Muslim-majority southern provinces since 2004, claiming more than 7,000 lives. The insurgency is primarily led by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional, which has sought greater autonomy from Buddhist-majority Thailand. The timing is notable: Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and cabinet members are scheduled to visit the southern region next week to discuss investment, flood prevention, and security.

stories.headline: Update: Sacked Ukrainian Defence Minister Calls on Zelensky to Answer Corruption Questions
stories.summary:
Mykhailo Fedorov, the Ukrainian defence minister fired last month after reportedly clashing with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, told the BBC that President Volodymyr Zelensky should be questioned about his awareness of corruption in his inner circle. Fedorov's remarks follow the announcement of a money laundering investigation by Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau into lawmakers and bankers, which Fedorov said raises legitimate questions about what the president knew. He was careful to note that he personally never witnessed Zelensky engage in corrupt activity.

Fedorov also renewed calls for elections to be held in Ukraine, arguing that democracy should not be "the hostage of Putin." Zelensky pushed back Sunday, saying wartime elections would be "a tsunami" that could split the country. Experts have noted significant practical obstacles to holding a vote, including how soldiers, millions of refugees abroad, and residents of occupied territories would participate.

The exchange marks a significant new development in Ukrainian domestic politics, with a popular and recently sacked minister publicly pressuring the wartime president on both corruption accountability and democratic legitimacy. Protests over Fedorov's dismissal had subsided by Wednesday after his replacement was confirmed, but his BBC interview and renewed calls for a wartime vote represent an escalation of political tension in Kyiv at a critical moment in the war.

stories.headline: Israel Strikes Syria Again Near Damascus; Washington Had Warned of "Unnecessary Escalation"
stories.summary:
Israel carried out a strike on the village of Beit Jinn, southwest of Damascus, targeting what the Israeli military described as a "terrorist" in the "final stages" of preparing attacks posing an immediate threat to soldiers. Syrian officials condemned the strike as a hit on a civilian vehicle that left several people injured, calling it a violation of Syrian sovereignty and international law. It was the second known Israeli strike on Syrian territory in a week.

The latest attack follows Israeli strikes earlier in the week on the Abu al-Duhur airbase near the Turkish border, which prompted a rare public rebuke from Washington. The U.S. ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, suggested the strikes could be Israel "baiting the Turks" ahead of upcoming Israeli elections — a characterization Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz rejected as "full of inaccuracies," insisting Israel acted on "clear intelligence information about Turkey's intentions."

The escalating strikes are straining relations between Israel, Syria's new government, and Turkey, which has provided military assistance to Damascus since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in 2024. Israel continues to occupy territory in southwest Syria seized after Assad's overthrow and views both Syria and Turkey with deep suspicion. Syria's new leadership has been building closer ties with the West, including a November 2025 White House visit by Syrian leader al-Sharaa, making Israel's repeated strikes a growing source of regional tension.
